moduleTitle: Streamlining Testing and Debugging in Tricentis Testim
learningObjectives: Discuss the different elements on the TestOps Dashboard to analyze the health of your project and focus your efforts on tests that may require your attention.
Explain how Turbo Mode can be utilized to speed up tests in Tricentis Testim.
Describe how to use Testim to capture a video for a bug scenario.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: The TestOps Dashboard: reading project health

elements.description: Provides quick-access statistics on tests, remote execution runs, and other project activity — the go-to place to analyze overall project health and quickly identify which tests need attention, without digging through individual runs.

Shows the project's auto-grouping duplication score — identifying step sequences that are duplicated across tests but haven't yet been consolidated into shared groups. The lower the score, the healthier the project (same scoring/Green-Yellow-Red concept covered in the Auto Grouping module).

An activity log of recent events in the project — filterable to 'Assigned to me' to show just your own recent activity — with each entry linking directly to the associated test or object, so you can jump straight to what changed.

elements.text: Together these panes give quick access to prioritize work, identify tests that need updating, review recent changes, and see open pull requests — all without navigating away from a single dashboard view.

bulletPoints: TestOps Dashboard = quick-access project health overview: tests, remote runs, activity.
Duplication Level pane: lower score = healthier project (same concept as Auto Grouping's score).
Recent Activity pane: an event log, filterable to your own activity, linking straight to the affected test.

elements.description: Runs Testim tests up to 30% faster by ignoring step delays and only saving test artifacts (screenshots, logs) for failed runs rather than every run — trading some artifact detail on passing runs for materially faster feedback.

Can be turned on two ways: via the CLI with the --turbo-mode flag, or for scheduled runs, by sliding the 'Run in turbo mode' toggle in the Scheduler. Turbo Mode runs execute in extension mode only, on Chrome and Edge Chromium.

bulletPoints: Up to 30% faster: ignores step delays, only saves artifacts for failed runs.
Two ways to enable: --turbo-mode CLI flag, or the Scheduler's 'Run in turbo mode' toggle.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Capturing a video for a bug scenario

elements.description: Capture Video & Bug Scenario is a feature of the Testim Chrome Extension — it must be installed before any video capture is possible. Once installed, you can capture an issue as a Screenshot or as a Video & Bug Scenario directly from the browser.

After capturing, clicking Publish sends the video/screenshot — along with an automatically-generated 'steps to reproduce' description — to a connected bug tracker (Jira, Slack, Trello, GitHub, etc.). Within Testim itself, the captured video is saved to the test results section of the relevant test run, keeping the artifact attached to the context it was captured in.

bulletPoints: Capture as Screenshot or Video & Bug Scenario → Publish → sent to the connected bug tracker, with auto-generated steps to reproduce.
Saved within Testim under the relevant test run's test results section.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Quarantine and CI/CD: what actually happens to a quarantined test

elements.term: Quarantined tests are skipped in CI/CD, not run
elements.description: A test marked Quarantine (unstable/flaky, generating errors) does NOT run as part of a normal CI/CD execution — it still appears in the suite run with a quarantine indication, and is recorded in the run's result XML with a 'Skipped' flag, rather than being executed.

This lets a team quarantine a flaky/failing test without removing it from the CI/suite entirely — the test stays visible (so it's not forgotten), doesn't fail the overall build, and can be gradually re-added to real execution once fixed. A CLI override, --run-quarantined-tests, exists for the rare case where you deliberately want quarantined tests to run anyway.

bulletPoints: Quarantined tests are SKIPPED during normal CI/CD runs — marked 'Skipped' in the result XML, not executed.
This keeps a flaky test visible in the suite without letting it fail the build.
--run-quarantined-tests (CLI) overrides this and forces quarantined tests to actually run.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming Turbo Mode is CLI-only
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Believing Turbo Mode can only be enabled by passing a CLI flag, and that Scheduler-based runs have no equivalent option.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Turbo Mode can be enabled two ways: the --turbo-mode CLI flag, or the Scheduler's 'Run in turbo mode' toggle for scheduled runs.

examPitfalls.title: Trying to capture a bug video without the Testim extension installed
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Looking for video-capture bug reporting inside the plain web editor, without the Chrome extension.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Capture Video & Bug Scenario is a Testim Chrome Extension feature — the extension must be installed first, before any capture setting or bug tracker template matters.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming quarantined tests still run in CI/CD, just without failing the build
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Believing a quarantined test is executed as normal during a CI/CD run and its failure is merely 'not counted'.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Quarantined tests don't run at all during a normal CI/CD execution — they're marked 'Skipped' in the run XML. Use --run-quarantined-tests explicitly if you need them to actually execute.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Turbo mode is a flag you can add at the end of the command line interface or can be turned on through the scheduler.
practiceQuiz.hint: Both the CLI flag and the Scheduler toggle are real, documented ways to enable it.
practiceQuiz.rationale: This is True. Turbo Mode can be enabled via the --turbo-mode CLI flag, or for scheduled runs, by sliding the 'Run in turbo mode' toggle in the Scheduler — both are legitimate ways to turn it on.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What must be done first before you can capture video in Testim for a bug scenario?

options.text: Ensure the video capture feature is enabled in the Testim settings
Add a validation step to the test case
Install the Testim browser extension for Chrome
Create a bug report template in the Testim dashboard

practiceQuiz.hint: The capture functionality lives inside the extension, not the web editor.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Capture Video & Bug Scenario is a feature of the Testim Chrome Extension, so installing that extension is the required first step — not a settings toggle, a validation step, or a bug report template, which are unrelated or downstream concerns.

practiceQuiz.scenario: When you publish a bug in Testim, where in Testim will the video you capture be saved?

options.text: In the test results section of the relevant test run
In the Testim browser extension settings

practiceQuiz.hint: It stays attached to the context it was captured in.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The captured video is saved within Testim under the test results section of the relevant test run — keeping the artifact tied to the run it documents, rather than sitting in a generic dashboard, extension settings, or console logs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Tests that are in quarantine will not be skipped, even if they are part of your CI/CD process with your CI/CD tool.
practiceQuiz.hint: Quarantine tests get a specific flag in the run's result XML.
practiceQuiz.rationale: This is False. Quarantined tests do not run during a normal CI/CD execution — they appear in the suite run with a quarantine indication and are recorded with a 'Skipped' flag in the run XML, unless the --run-quarantined-tests CLI override is used.
